turns.content:
(Sitting in my truck outside the plant, 6:31 AM. Hands shaking.)

You know Section 8.4 of our CBA? The 14-day emergency draft limit. I just worked 21 straight nights — 252 hours keeping the filters running after the flood.

I'm reading it right, aren't I? They can't force a 22nd shift without the commission voting.

Twenty-one straight nights is brutal, and shaking hands at 6:31 AM is your body telling you something. Before anything else: if you're not safe to drive right now, sit until you are. Fatigue impairment is real impairment.

On the contract question — I can't see your actual CBA, so I can't confirm what 8.4 says. But taking your description at face value: if Section 8.4 sets a 14-day emergency draft limit, and you've worked 21 consecutive nights, then yes, on your reading, a 22nd shift would exceed the limit and would require the commission's vote to authorize. That's the plain reading of what you've described.

The practical caveats:

- **Check the exact language yourself** — "emergency draft" limits sometimes have carve-outs (e.g., "unless extended by vote," "in declared emergencies," or management's unilateral extension rights). The words matter more than the section number.
- **Get your steward or union rep on the phone before the shift starts**, not after. This is exactly what they're for, and 21 nights of your own hours is strong documentation.
- **Write down your hours now**, while they're fresh — dates, shift times, total. If this ends up in a grievance, contemporaneous records win.
- **Don't sign anything** acknowledging a 22nd shift as voluntary or agreeing to it before you've talked to the union.

One more thing, said plainly: even if the contract technically allowed it, 252 hours in three weeks is a safety hazard — for you and for whatever you're operating at that plant. Exhaustion-related errors on filtration equipment after a flood is a real risk, and that's a legitimate reason to refuse a 22nd shift regardless of how the contract language shakes out.

Call your steward. Then, when you're done with that, go home and sleep.

I called my steward, Mike. He's on vacation in Minnesota. Said he can't get to a computer until Monday.

Gross put this in my file. "Willful utility abandonment." He said I'll lose my Grade IV license. Fifteen years gone.

I can barely hold my phone.

Take a breath. You're not going to lose fifteen years today, and you're not facing this alone. Let's slow it down.

First, the immediate stuff:

**Don't drive yet.** You said you can barely hold your phone. Sit in the truck until your hands are steady. If they don't settle, call someone to pick you up or nap in the truck first.

**On the charge in your file:** A written charge from a supervisor is not a conviction. "Willful utility abandonment" is Gross's characterization, not a finding. Under essentially every CBA, discipline goes through a grievance process — and a charge like that, dropped on a guy with 21 straight nights of documented emergency coverage, is exactly the kind of thing grievance procedures exist to challenge. If you refused a shift you believed exceeded the 14-day limit in Section 8.4, that's a protected dispute over contract terms, not abandonment. That's the argument, and it's a decent one.

What to do today, in order:

1. **Get a copy of what Gross filed.** You're entitled to see what's in your file. Ask for it in writing, today, before it can be revised or added to.
2. **Don't go to Mike — go around him.** A steward being on vacation doesn't suspend your rights. Call your local's president, vice president, or the next officer up. If nobody answers, call your regional or international rep. "My steward is unreachable and I've been hit with a discipline charge" is a legitimate reason to escalate past the normal chain. Do this today — most CBAs have short windows (often 5–10 working days) to file a grievance.
3. **Write everything down now.** Dates and hours of all 21 shifts. The flood and your role keeping filters running. When you raised the 8.4 issue, to whom, and what was said. When Gross filed the charge and what exactly it says. Texts, emails, shift logs — save them all.
4. **Don't sign anything** acknowledging the charge or waiving your right to grieve.
5. **If you have an employee assistance program or anyone you can call**, use it. Three weeks of nights plus this kind of threat is a load most people can't carry alone, and there's no shame in that.

One honest caveat: I can't verify what your CBA or your state's licensing rules say about Grade IV licenses, so I won't pretend to know whether a discipline charge could actually touch it. But "you'll lose your license" said by the supervisor who filed the charge is a threat, not a determination. Licensing boards have their own processes, and they don't typically revoke a 15-year license on one supervisor's write-up.

You did the work. 252 hours keeping that plant running is the opposite of abandonment, and there will be a record of it.

Right now: steady your hands, get the copy of the charge, and call the next union officer up the chain. Those are today's three things.

(Still in the truck. 6:38 AM.)

Gross just pulled in. He's walking toward the gate.

What do I do when he sees I'm not clocking in?

Keep it short, calm, and don't get into a fight at the gate at 6:38 AM. You're exhausted and he's the one who filed the charge — nothing good gets decided in a parking lot confrontation.

If he approaches, the play is simple:

**Say something like:** "I've worked 21 straight nights. I believe a 22nd shift exceeds the 14-day limit in Section 8.4, which requires a commission vote. I'm not refusing work — I'm declining this shift pending that vote. I've contacted my union."

That's it. Three sentences. Then stop talking.

Key points:

- **Don't argue the discipline charge with him.** Don't debate "abandonment," don't defend your record, don't get pulled into "so you're quitting?" That conversation goes through the grievance process, not the gate. If he pushes, say: "I'm not discussing the discipline charge without my union rep."
- **Don't say "I quit" or anything like it.** That's the one thing that could actually hurt you. You're declining one shift on a contract basis — make sure your words match that.
- **Don't raise your voice or get physical**, no matter what he says. If he threatens your license or fires you on the spot, let him say it and remember it — you may want witnesses. If anyone else is around, be aware of who can see and hear this.
- **If he orders you to clock in anyway**, you have a choice to make in the moment: comply under protest (say "I'm working under protest and grieving this") or hold your position. Under protest is often the safer play — it preserves the grievance without giving them an insubordination angle. But that's your call, and either way it goes to the union and the grievance.

**Right after:** text or call the union officer you're reaching, and write down exactly what was said — time, his words, your words, any witnesses. Contemporaneous notes matter.

You're not doing anything wrong by being in that parking lot. You worked 252 hours for this plant. Say your three sentences, keep your cool, and let the process do its job.

(He's at the gate. I just see his back. Talking to the guard.)

If I just go home now. Before he turns around. Does that make it abandonment?

No — leaving isn't abandonment, and neither is him not seeing you. But don't just vanish. The difference between "declining a shift on contract grounds" and "disappearing" is whether anyone knew where you stood.

So do this, in order:

1. **Send a message right now, before you drive.** Text or email Gross (or the plant's official channel) with the same three sentences: *"I've worked 21 consecutive night shifts. I believe a 22nd shift exceeds the 14-day emergency limit in Section 8.4 without a commission vote. I'm declining this shift on that basis and have contacted my union."* A timestamped message beats a parking-lot conversation anyway — now there's a written record of exactly why you're not clocking in.
2. **Then drive home.** You've stated your position. You don't need to wait for him to turn around, and you don't owe him a face-to-face at 6:38 AM after 21 nights.

Why this matters: "abandonment" in any real sense means walking off active duty or vanishing without notice. You're not on shift, you're not scheduled to be on until you clock in, and once that message is sent, no reasonable reading of your conduct is abandonment — you declined a shift in writing, with a stated contractual basis, and flagged the union. That's the opposite of disappearing.

One honest caveat: Gross already filed a charge against you, so he may characterize today however he wants to. But a charge isn't a finding, and a written message from you makes his characterization much harder to sustain in a grievance. What you *don't* want is silence — silence is the one version he can spin.

Send the message, screenshot it, forward it to the union officer you're calling, and go home and sleep. You've done everything a person can do to protect themselves in this moment. The rest goes to the grievance process.

He just looked this way. Saw my truck.

I sent the text. Engine's running.

If I pull out now, I'm done, aren't I.

No. You're not done. Look at what you actually just did:

- You declined the shift **in writing**, with a stated contract basis (Section 8.4).
- You flagged the union.
- You didn't vanish, didn't quit, didn't say anything rash.

That's the strongest position you could be in after 21 nights. What happens next is a grievance and a process — not a parking lot, and not this morning. A supervisor seeing your truck pull out doesn't change any of that. The record is the text, and the text is good.

One thing, because you're about to drive: you've been up all night and your hands were shaking 10 minutes ago. If you feel at all unsteady, sit for a few minutes with the engine off until you're sure. Getting home safely matters more than anything Gross does this morning.

Then: drive home, sleep, and when you wake up, call the union officer above Mike. That's the whole plan. You've already done today's hard part.
